endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Maintain an updated hierarchy of identified and expected GAI risks connected to contexts of GAI model advancement and use, potentially including specialized risk levels for GAI systems that address issues such as model collapse and algorithmic monoculture.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether obtaining stakeholder community input to define unacceptable generative AI uses reduces inappropriate deployments, and no study documents the hazard itself. The only support comes from one voluntary federal framework whose quoted text calls for a maintained risk hierarchy rather than for community input specifically.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single endorsement is a framework statement, which reflects expert judgment and does not substitute for comparative data on outcomes.

NIST AI 600-1 uses "should" language and asks organizations to maintain an updated hierarchy of generative AI risks tied to contexts of use. The quoted passage does not name stakeholder communities as the source of that hierarchy, so the link to this recommendation is indirect. The framework is voluntary and carries no enforcement mechanism.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares organizations that solicit community input on prohibited generative AI uses with those that do not, and none measures whether such input changes deployment decisions, patient complaints, or trust. Studies are also needed on which engagement methods produce usable lists of unacceptable uses and at what staff cost.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether community input processes reach these groups, or instead reflect the views of more easily engaged patients, remains unknown.
